skill.name: ai-runtime-toolkit
skill.description: Discovers, documents, and runs AI Runtime helper tools for CLI integration, system checks, API testing, and project analysis.
skill.summary: Manage AI Runtime CLI tools for discovery, execution, monitoring, and analysis.
skill.author: Dwsy

security_audit.summary: The skill intentionally exposes local tool execution, network checks, and filesystem inspection. Most obfuscation, prompt-injection, path-traversal, and key-file alerts are false positives from documentation or localized text. Real risks remain in remote pipe-to-shell install guidance, privileged install commands, direct .env sourcing, and metadata-driven tool execution.

remediation.issue: Remote install commands are piped directly into sh.
remediation.suggestion: Replace pipe-to-shell instructions with package-manager steps, pinned release downloads, and checksum verification.

remediation.issue: Documentation includes sudo package and keyring modification commands.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user confirmation and link to official installation docs instead of encouraging automatic privileged execution.
Parse only required keys safely or require explicit environment variables without executing project-controlled shell content.

remediation.issue: The CLI runs discovered tool files through a generic runner.
remediation.suggestion: Add a fixed allowlist, path containment checks, executable ownership checks, and a confirmation prompt before running tools.

remediation.issue: Filesystem helpers can scan broad local paths and temporary directories.
remediation.suggestion: Default to scoped project paths, warn before root or system-log scans, and avoid shared temporary files for sensitive output.

content.user_title: Run AI Runtime CLI Toolkits Safely
content.value_statement: Teams need a consistent way to discover and run CLI helpers across projects. This skill organizes AI Runtime tools for discovery, execution, monitoring, and analysis.
actual_capabilities: Discovers internal tools from metadata files and displays tool details.
Lists external CLI tools such as fzf, eza, bat, ripgrep, zoxide, jq, and xh.
Runs bundled internal tools through a Python command-line wrapper.
Provides Bash helpers for log analysis, disk health, and service checks.
Includes a Node API tester for REST endpoints and report output.
Documents how to add tools and integrate third-party CLIs.
limitations: Some install guidance uses privileged commands or remote shell scripts that require manual review.
Shell helpers can read local logs, directories, and environment files when run.
External tool detection depends on tools being installed and available on PATH.
The toolkit does not sandbox tool execution or validate every target path.

use_cases.title: Validate Deployment Health
use_cases.description: Run service, disk, and API checks after a deployment using the bundled helper tools.

use_cases.title: Inspect Project Tooling
use_cases.description: List available internal and external tools before choosing the best helper for a task.

use_cases.title: Maintain Tool Documentation
use_cases.description: Review metadata, usage examples, and integration guides for an AI Runtime toolkit.

prompt_templates.title: List Available Tools
prompt_templates.prompt: Show the available AI Runtime toolkit tools, grouped by internal and external tools. Include each tool purpose and any missing dependencies.

prompt_templates.title: Run A Health Check
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the service and disk health tools to check this project environment. Ask before running commands that need network, sudo, or broad filesystem access.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze Project Support
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this project and recommend which AI Runtime toolkit tools could help. Explain the task, expected output, and risk for each recommendation.

prompt_templates.title: Harden Toolkit Usage
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit the toolkit usage and documentation for unsafe install commands, environment file handling, and broad path scans. Suggest safer alternatives.

output_examples.input: List the toolkit tools available for service diagnostics.
output_examples.output: A grouped summary of service checks, disk checks, log analysis, API testing, required dependencies, and suggested next commands.

output_examples.input: Review the external tool integration guide for safe installation.
output_examples.output: A short audit that flags remote shell installers, sudo package commands, shell startup changes, and safer manual installation steps.

output_examples.input: Recommend tools for investigating API failures in a local project.
output_examples.output: A concise plan using API tests, service health checks, and log analysis, with expected evidence and required permissions.

best_practices: Review all install commands before running remote scripts or privileged package manager commands.
Run bundled tools with least privilege and scoped project paths.
Keep metadata files accurate so discovery and recommendations match real tool behavior.
anti_patterns: Do not run pipe-to-shell install commands automatically from documentation or metadata.
Do not source untrusted environment files from a project directory.
Do not scan broad paths such as root or system logs unless the user explicitly requests it.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps discover, document, and run AI Runtime helper tools for CLI workflows, monitoring, API testing, and analysis.

faq.question: Does it install external tools automatically?
faq.answer: No. The documentation includes install guidance, but remote scripts and privileged commands should require manual approval.

faq.question: Can it run local commands?
faq.answer: Yes. The toolkit includes Bash, Python, and Node tools that execute local commands when the user runs them.

faq.question: Does it need network access?
faq.answer: Some tools test local or configured HTTP endpoints. External install examples also reference remote URLs.

faq.question: Can it read sensitive files?
faq.answer: Some helpers can read logs, directories, and environment files. Use scoped paths and avoid untrusted environment files.

faq.question: Who should use it?
faq.answer: It is best for developers and platform teams that already manage AI Runtime tooling and need structured CLI workflows.
